items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Eddie Gomez, who I’d worked with, done some session work with... So, I asked Eddie if he wanted to play with us... we went in the studio and recorded “New Directions”

ctx.x: Monk, yeah. So when he had his label I talked to him about doing my own record and he said to me, “Well, think about what you want to do and you get it together. Come to me and do it.” I’ll say one of my mentors who I really had a lot of fun with when I came to New York and was really great was Roy Haynes. So Roy Haynes and I used to hang out. Still stay in touch with each other a lot. I used to call him “Papa Daddy.” So I wrote this piece for him. I played the melodica so I decided I’d like to do a melodica/drum…
We’re going to run out of tape here quickly but I just wanted to ask. So when you did the recording with Miles in November of 68’ were you officially a member of the band at that point?

items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: I think Joanne Brackeen wrote some very challenging music for Eddie Gomez.

ctx.x: think you probably always bring your A game but do you recall a situation where you felt really challenged?

Well you know when I play more arranged music, you know, I have the artist send me an audio version of what they have in mind and send me the music. And so I spend time with that so when I get to the studio I’m ready to go. I know the arrangement without having a read it. So that’s what I do with challenging music. I think Joanne Brackeen wrote some very challenging music for Eddie Gomez. She writes a lot of chords and a lot of chords that move fairly fast. Two bars, two beats, one bar. So that was really…

That’s a very interesting answer because I would have assumed that the challenge might have been more along the lines of no arrangements, as if this is going to be open to where you want to go. So I really appreciate you enlightening me about that.
